content: CD69, also known as Cluster of Differentiation 69, is a transmembrane C-type lectin protein encoded by the CD69 gene. It serves as an early activation marker and is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells, T cells, and various other immune cell types. CD69 plays a role in T cell differentiation and in retaining lymphocytes within lymphoid organs. When T lymphocytes or natural killer (NK) cells are activated, either in vivo or in vitro, CD69 expression is induced. CD69 is one of the earliest inducible glycoproteins expressed on the cell surface during lymphocyte activation. It is involved in lymphocyte proliferation and functions as a receptor that transmits signals in lymphocytes, NK cells, and platelets. The CD69 gene is located in the NK gene complex on chromosome 6 in mice and chromosome 12 in humans. Activation of signaling pathways in lymphocytes, NK cells, dendritic cells, and other immune cells leads to the upregulation of transcription factors such as NF-κB, ERG-1, and AP-1, which promote CD69 gene transcription. The CD69 protein undergoes post-translational modifications, including differential glycosylation, resulting in either a 28 kDa or 32 kDa peptide. These peptides form a homodimer linked by a disulfide bond. Each subunit contains a C-type lectin domain (CTLD) for ligand binding, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic tail for intracellular signaling. Unlike typical CTLDs, CD69 lacks calcium-binding residues, suggesting it binds proteins rather than carbohydrates. CD69 has been shown to bind ligands such as Galectin-1 (Gal-1) and Myl9/12, though additional ligands remain unidentified. Ligand binding activates signaling pathways, including the Jak/Stat and mTOR/HIF1-α pathways. CD69 also interacts with S1P and LAT1 receptors, influencing lymphocyte egress and other immune responses. Further research is needed to fully elucidate CD69-ligand interactions and its intracellular signaling mechanisms. CD69 expression is associated with the differentiation of regulatory T cells (Tregs), memory T cells, and Bcl6^loCD69^hi light zone germinal center B cell plasmablast precursors. Treg precursors leave the thymus expressing CD69 and complete their differentiation in peripheral tissues upon encountering antigens and cytokines such as IL-2. CD69 activation via the JAK/STAT pathway induces the production of TGF-β and IL-2, which are critical for Treg differentiation. Additionally, CD69 is upregulated by NF-κB signaling during the early stages of an immune response. A prolonged immune response is maintained by the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, which is also linked to Treg differentiation. CD69 is a marker for both precursor and mature tissue-resident memory T cells (TRMs) in peripheral tissues. TGF-β plays a role in TRM differentiation, similar to its role in Treg differentiation. Most lymphocytes express sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1P1-5), which are G protein-coupled receptors that bind sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), a sphingolipid metabolite abundant in the bloodstream. S1P binding to S1P1 promotes lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs to affected tissues. However, when T cells are activated in lymphoid organs via cytokine and TCR signaling, CD69 is expressed and forms a complex with S1P1. This interaction depends on the CD69 transmembrane domain and helix-4 of S1P1. The CD69-S1P1 complex leads to the internalization and degradation of S1P1, preventing it from binding S1P and initiating downstream signaling. This results in temporary retention of lymphocytes within lymphoid organs, which may enhance the likelihood of successful lymphocyte activation, particularly if the initial activation signal was weak. Research suggests that CD69 and S1P1 co-regulate each other. When CD69 is more abundant, it reduces S1P1 membrane localization, while higher S1P1 levels decrease CD69 membrane localization. This reciprocal regulation of CD69 and S1P1 impacts lymphocyte egress and migration.
